story_text.value:
Hello HN,

I am the founder of a small nonprofit which built Museum of Ages. We opened its first wing last week, a digital Leonardo da Vinci museum. It is a virtual tour with 17 stops, his works and then his last house in Amboise. The entrance is free.

At the different stops you can see for example his paintings close to their real size, or 15 of his machines rebuilt in code, and you can have a look at 29 of his anatomy sheets. We also selected 207 of his manuscript pages which you can read in a virtual reading table, mirror the view to read his writing and 131 of the 207 are translated. We also rebuilt his last house in Amboise on the later stops of the walk. The museum is available in seven languages.

Each stop has one of four grades as a label, documented, reconstructed, conjectural and not known. In a detailed view the user can have a closer look at the sources.

The materials of the rooms and machines are created in Three.js. The museum runs with WebGPU. If the browser doesn’t support it, the fallback is WebGL2. To create the textures we used Creative Commons Zero photo scans (CC0) and for a few small objects we use free 3D models (CC0).

Our mission is to create digital museums you can walk as not everyone can get to a museum, because illness or disability keeps them away. Some cannot afford the trip or just reside far away. So our goal is also to make our digital museums as accessible as possible. Therefore we also pre-rendered the walk so that it also works on older phones and is easy to use for older people.

We released the code under AGPL-3.0. The texts and pictures are CC BY-SA 4.0. Reproductions have their own licenses. https://github.com/chipmates/museumofages

We put a lot of time and passion into the museum and hope you like it. We are happy about any feedback. Which digital museum would you like to see next?

story_text.value:
Video as code took off with the Opus 5.5 release. People now make videos by writing code, with Remotion, HyperFrames and others.

We wanted the same for 3D videos. You can use something like Blender, but it's heavy to install and slow to render.

So we made ManimGX:

- Lightweight: a 65–110 MB download, depending on the OS

- Easy to install: pip install manimgx (Python 3.13+), with no system dependencies

- Cross-platform: macOS, Windows and Linux, and even the browser via Pyodide and WebGPU

- Blazingly fast: a Rust + wgpu engine, 90.6× faster than Manim CE and 18.7× faster than Blender Workbench, from launch to finished MP4

- Compatible with Manim Community Edition's API, with LaTeX and Typst math built in

Now it's much easier for anyone with a coding agent to make 3D computer graphics videos.

Repo: https://github.com/academa-labs/manimgx

Docs: https://manimgx.academa.ai

X post: https://x.com/sinaatalay/status/2109045945149395421

Happy to answer any questions!

story_text.value:
Hello HN, I'm Lucas and I work as a front-end developer. GSS (GPU Style Sheets) is a language for Those people who already know CSS and who want to create 3D effects without first learning GLSL.

You declare shapes in an @scene block, style them with selectors, and the compiler turns the whole stylesheet into one fragment shader: signed distance fields, It was implemented using WebGL2, or through WebGPU (using WGSL) with a fallback to WebGL2. Three.js was not used, nor was it. meshes, no UVs. ``` @scene { torus#ring; sphere#ball; } #ball { color: #ff5a36; radius: .55; material: jelly(.6); } animation: float 2s ease-in-out alternate; } ```

What carries over from CSS, with the same behavior: specificity and the cascade, Important: nesting with &, combinators, and :hover/:active with transition, @keyframes and every easing (cubic-bezier, linear(), steps), calc()/clamp()/trig, custom properties and @property, oklch()/color-mix(), gradients, @media (live), Animations driven by scrolling, with offset-path. Since CSS or SVG already have such a concept, GSS copies its syntax instead of inventing one (noise() is modeled on The turbulence is processed by means of displace() on the feDisplacementMap, and the prism or lathe takes a path.

How it works: the compiler (TypeScript, runs in the browser or at build time via a Vite plugin) resolves the cascade per object, then emits an SDF per shape Put them together. The animations are assessed in the shader, not in JavaScript. Objects are arranged in space, with those far away being omitted on a per-ray basis. A scene that doesn't move doesn't redraw.

How to use it: include a <gss-scene src="x.gss"> tag from a CDN and mount(canvas, source) from npm, or precompile with Vite (the runtime is ~15 KB gzipped; the compiler About 110 KB when you compile it onto the page).

The latest version is 0.0.5 and SDFs do not support mesh or glTF imports. Raymarching is expensive on weak integrated GPUs (without a GPU, a scene waits for a click Rather than freezing the page) the scene obscures the page behind it.

Playground: https://www.gss-lang.dev/playground Docs: https://www.gss-lang.dev/docs Code (Apache-2.0): https://github.com/LukyVj/GSS

I'd love feedback on the language design: where the CSS analogy holds, and The point at which it breaks or is misleading.

story_text.value:
Hi,

I’m launching the COLMAP browser workspace today!

offlinetools.io/colmap

It’s a free and fully local browser implementation of the popular open-source photogrammetry software COLMAP.

No download, no sign-up, no installation, no setup, no cloud processing — everything happens and stays on the user’s machine.

More info: offlinetools.io/colmap-landing

Why is it relevant? Bringing COLMAP to the browser is technically challenging because of the browser’s additional constraints.

This is the first implementation that reaches native-class performance and, in some cases, even outperforms the native build.

It produces standard COLMAP-compatible outputs such as camera poses, sparse point clouds, keypoints and masks for downstream workflows including Gaussian Splatting.

The local nature of this tool makes it ideal for data-sensitive verticals such as police, medical, law enforcement, insurance, or simply users who want the tool but don't want to bother with installs and cloud.

About me: I’m a former Google engineer with around 20 years of experience in 3D computer vision.

story_text.value:
Semi inspired by the 3d Shinjuku station that was posted again recently, I noticed it was missing a large portion of the "complex" where "complex" is defined loosly has how far you can walk without stepping outside.

So I asked Claude to make a 3d map of all Tokyo Trains, no libraries, and let you zoom into stations, and the first version with both map and the Shinjuku complex was ready in about 3 hours. It spent another 7 or so in various nit picky things I asked for to get to the current version.

I know these will only get better but I think the thing I find most interesting is no libraries needed. Claude can write the shaders from scratch, it can do both WebGPU and WebGL, and it can often write optimal solutions. For example, the entire map/station/trains is rendered in 5 draw calls. I didn't ask for that, it just did it.

This one has lots of imprefections. Most of that comes down to data and/or deciding how to use the data provided. For example, AFAICT there is nothing that says "these parts make the complex". It's something you either need to derive or hand code rules/lists (include this, don't include that).

Anyway, I know not everyone is into it but I'm having fun.

story_text.value:
Hey HN! We’ve been working on this project for almost 3 years now, and recently decided to finally make it open source.

It’s a local-first video editor that runs in the browser and is mostly built from scratch. We’re using WebCodecs for all the encoding and decoding work, which lets us get performance pretty close to native editors.

Since day one the goal of the project was to solve LLM-based video editing, but the models have only recently become capable enough to make it genuinely useful. Instead of trying to force our own chat interface onto users, we built a CLI that is designed to work with existing coding agents like Claude Code.

The idea is that agents can operate the editor directly, while you can still open the same project in a visual interface to review their work and change things yourself.

A few things that set it apart from other NLEs: - The editor is an infinite canvas (kind of like Figma, but for video editing) - You can build compositions as SolidJS modules and mount them through the CLI - Editing and rendering happen locally. The editor can render both HTML and GPU native entities - Everything that runs on your device is completely free, including 4K/60 fps exports, unlimited projects, and no footage duration limit - Your footage stays on your device unless you explicitly use one of our analysis services. For transcription, we only upload the audio track

So when it’s open source, how do we intend to finance future development?

Coding agents don’t include every backend service they need to understand footage and make accurate editing decisions. We provide optional services like transcription, multimodal understanding, and object tracking, which we bill with a small margin.

What can agents currently do with the editor? - A lot of common post-production work: social media edits, captions, color grading, zoom effects, and animations - We recently added support for the html-in-canvas API, which turned out to be really useful for creating serious motion graphics - Video and audio understanding. For example, you can ask an agent to find certain scenes, summarize a YouTube video, or identify the relevant parts of a longer recording.

There’s still quite a lot we want to build. A few of the bigger things on our backlog: - Agentic edits based on beats and other audio characteristics - Native 3D capabilities - A full WebGPU renderer - A native color-grading UI

Would love to get some feedback & happy to answer any questions!
